While a client is connected, the processor copies a configurable slice of the
telemetry passing through it into local, zstd-compressed OTLP files, and the
client pulls the files over gRPC. Every batch is passed on unchanged. With no
client connected, it only passes data on. It's meant for debugging sessions
of an hour or two: you record, then query the files with DuckDB and the
[duckdb-otlp](https://github.com/smithclay/duckdb-otlp) extension, or any
tool that reads OTLP.

It can go anywhere in a pipeline, and more than once, for example before and
after a filter to see what the filter removed.

Clients are separate programs. Any program that speaks
[the protocol](#the-pull-protocol) can pull.

## How it protects the pipeline

- It never changes the batch it passes on, and never returns an error.
- When no client is recording, it passes each batch on after one check, and
  copies nothing.
- It never waits for its disk. Kept records are marshaled, put in a buffer,
  and compressed and written by four writer goroutines per signal, each with
  its own file. The buffer holds at most `max_buffer_mib`. When it's full,
  the next batch isn't copied at all, and its records are counted as
  skipped. A burst bigger than the buffer, such as one huge trace arriving
  within seconds, loses records this way. Raise `max_buffer_mib` if the
  counters show it.
- If it can't start its server, or can't create or measure its directory
  when a client starts recording, it logs an error and only passes data on.
  The collector still starts.
- Its disk use is bounded by `max_disk_mib`. At the limit, it copies nothing
  until the client has pulled enough files.
- A `where` condition that fails to evaluate counts as false. The OTTL library
  may log each failure.

## Configuration

```yaml
processors:
  remotetap:
    directory: /var/lib/otelcol/tap
    max_disk_mib: 1024
    max_file_mib: 64
    traces:
      rules:
        # Full detail for every checkout span.
        - where: ['resource.attributes["service.name"] == "checkout"']
          detail: full
        # Full detail for 5% of whole traces.
        - trace_percent: 5
          detail: full
        # Attribute keys and sizes for everything else.
        - detail: keys
    logs:
      rules:
        - detail: sizes
    metrics:
      rules:
        - where: ['metric.name == "http.server.request.duration"']
          detail: keys
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `directory` | required | Where sessions are written until a client pulls them |
| `max_disk_mib` | `1024` | Total size of everything in `directory`. While it's reached, the tap copies nothing, until the client has pulled enough files. It can be about one batch per writer over. |
| `max_buffer_mib` | `64` | Memory for copies waiting to be written. While it's full, the tap copies nothing, and counts what it skipped. |
| `max_file_mib` | `64` | Uncompressed size at which a file is closed and a new one started. At most 95, because duckdb-otlp reads files of up to 100 MB after they're decompressed. A file is also closed after 10 seconds, so the client gets data soon. |
| `grpc` | `endpoint: 127.0.0.1:8866` | The server clients pull from, with the usual gRPC server options, such as `tls` and `auth`. Taps in one collector with the same endpoint share one server. |
| `traces`, `logs`, `metrics` | none | Rules for each signal. A signal without rules is only passed on. |

By default, the server only listens on localhost, so a client reaches it
through a tunnel. See [the pull protocol](#the-pull-protocol), and the
[security best practices](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/security/config-best-practices/#protect-against-denial-of-service-attacks)
before changing the endpoint.

A rule has:

- `where`: OTTL conditions, all of which must be true. Paths must start with
  their context: `span.`, `log.`, `metric.`, `datapoint.`, `resource.`, or
  `scope.`. A condition that fails to evaluate counts as false.
- `trace_percent`: keep this percentage of traces, chosen by hashing the trace
  ID. Every instance makes the same choice, so a kept trace is complete across
  instances. Logs without a trace ID never match. Not allowed for metrics.
- `detail`: `sizes`, `keys`, or `full`.

A record is kept when at least one rule matches. When several match, the
highest detail wins.

## Detail levels

Every level writes valid OTLP. The processor rewrites its own copy of each
kept record:

| Level | Written |
| --- | --- |
| `sizes` | Attributes, span events and links, exemplars, and log bodies are removed |
| `keys` | Each attribute value, and each log body, is replaced by a map: `{type: Str, bytes: 48930}`. Numbers, booleans, and strings and byte values of up to 32 bytes are kept, because the map would take about as much space. Maps and slices are always replaced. |
| `full` | The record is unchanged |

At every level the processor adds the `tap.*` attributes below, measured
before anything was removed.

At `keys`, short values such as namespaces, HTTP methods, and status codes
are kept, but so are short user IDs, email addresses, and IP addresses. Use
`sizes` where attribute values mustn't leave the collector.

## The tap.* attributes

These are defined in [`conventions.go`](conventions.go), which is the only
definition of the format.

| Attribute | On | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tap.session_id` | resource | The session that wrote the record |
| `tap.instance` | resource | The host name of the collector that wrote it |
| `tap.processor` | resource | The component ID of the tap that wrote it, such as `remotetap/after_filter` |
| `tap.resource_bytes` | resource | Encoded size of the original resource |
| `tap.schema_url` | resource, scope | The resource's or scope's schema URL, which says which semantic conventions it follows. OTLP has it, but duckdb-otlp doesn't show it. |
| `tap.detail` | record | `sizes`, `keys`, or `full` |
| `tap.rules` | record | Indexes of the rules that matched, in configuration order |
| `tap.attribute_count` | record | Number of attributes on the original record |
| `tap.span_bytes`, `tap.log_bytes`, `tap.point_bytes` | record | Encoded size of the original span, log record, or data point |
| `tap.event_count`, `tap.link_count` | span | Number of events and links on the original span |
| `tap.body_bytes` | log record | Approximate size of the original body |

Value sizes at the `keys` level, and `tap.body_bytes`, are approximate. They're
meant for comparing values with each other.

## The pull protocol

A client records by opening a gRPC stream to the collector, and pulls the
files the taps write. The protocol is
[`internal/tappb/tap.proto`](internal/tappb/tap.proto), and clients generate
their own code from it. Clients reach the collector however they like:
directly, or through a tunnel such as `ssh -L 8866:localhost:8866 host`,
`kubectl port-forward`, or `oc port-forward`.

- A stream starts with `Start`, which names the client, the taps to record,
  and the files the client already has part of. While a stream is open,
  every tap it asked for records. When the stream ends without `Stop`, the
  taps keep recording for a minute, so a client that reconnects finds no gap.
- The collector sends each file once it's complete, in chunks. Files never
  change once they're complete: see [Files](#files). The client checks each
  file's SHA-256, stores it, and acknowledges it. Only then does the collector
  delete it.
- A dropped connection loses nothing. The client reconnects with the same
  client ID, says how much of each file it has, and gets only the rest. A
  file the client has whole, but whose acknowledgement was lost, gets only
  its checksum. Keepalive pings notice a dead connection within about 15
  seconds.
- One client records a collector at a time. Another client is refused while a
  stream is open. A stream from the same client takes over from an older one,
  which is often still open because its connection died unnoticed.
- After `Stop`, the collector stops recording, sends what's left, and sends
  `Done` once every file has been acknowledged.

Anyone who can reach the endpoint can start recording and read what's
recorded. With the default endpoint, that's anyone who can reach the
collector's host, or port-forward to its pod.

## Files

Each signal of each processor writes its own session. A session starts when a
client starts recording, and stops when the client stops, or when its grace
period ends. `max_disk_mib` applies to everything in `directory` together:
unpulled files from earlier sessions, and every session this collector is
writing there, whatever its signal or processor.

```
/var/lib/otelcol/tap/
  20260926T081500Z-traces-a3f9/
    session.json             written once: rules, limits, and when it started
    traces-000001.pb.zst     OTLP protobuf, compressed with zstd
    traces-000002.pb.zst.tmp still being written; readers skip it
    stats-000001.json        counters and gauges, every 15 seconds
```

Every file is written once and never changed, so the client can pull each one
as soon as it appears, and a copy is never out of date. A file is written
under a temporary name and renamed when it's complete.

Batches are appended to a data file one after another, through one zstd
stream. Protobuf reads appended messages back as a single message, so each
file decompresses to one OTLP export request. A data file is renamed from
`.tmp` when it's complete: after `max_file_mib`, after 10 seconds, at the disk
limit, or when the session stops. On synthetic test data, compressed files
took 16 to 93 bytes per record, depending on the signal and detail level.

A pulled file is deleted from `directory`. A session's directory is deleted
once it has stopped and every file has been pulled.

### Stats snapshots

Every 15 seconds, whatever the files do, and once more when the session
stops, the session writes the next `stats-NNNNNN.json`, like a Prometheus
scrape, so a client can show them as time series. A snapshot holds:

- `time`, and `status`: `running`, or `stopped` in the last one, with
  `stop_reason` (`client_stop`, `client_gone`, `write_error`, or
  `shutdown`) and `stop_error`.
- `files`: the data files closed since the previous snapshot, with each
  one's size on disk, uncompressed size, and record count. Every data file is
  in exactly one snapshot. The collector sends a snapshot only after the
  files it lists.
- `gauges`: `buffer_bytes`, what's waiting to be written, and `disk_bytes`,
  everything in `directory`, as `max_disk_mib` counts it.
- `counters`, since the session started:

| Counter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `records_seen` | Records that reached the tap while it was recording |
| `records_skipped` | Records in batches that weren't copied, because the buffer was full |
| `records_disk_full` | Records in batches that weren't copied, because `max_disk_mib` was reached |
| `records_kept` | Records that matched a rule and were copied |
| `records_dropped` | Kept records that were never written: the buffer filled up, the disk limit was reached before they were written, or a write failed |
| `records_written` | Records in closed files |
| `batches_dropped` | Batches behind `records_dropped` |
| `bytes_written` | Size on disk of the closed files |
| `rule_matches` | Records each rule matched, in configuration order |

In the last snapshot, `records_kept` equals `records_written` plus
`records_dropped`.

### After a crash

If the collector crashes, the session has no stopped snapshot, and its
snapshots stop coming. The file that was being written is left as `.tmp`,
and is never renamed. Every other file in the session is complete, and the
next client pulls it. The leftover `.tmp` file counts toward `max_disk_mib`
until you delete it.

## Querying

Decompress the files first: duckdb-otlp doesn't read compressed files.

```sh
zstd -d --rm */*.pb.zst
```

Then query them with DuckDB:

```sql
INSTALL otlp FROM community;
LOAD otlp;

-- The biggest spans, whatever their detail level.
SELECT service_name, name,
       CAST(json_extract(span_attributes, '$."tap.span_bytes"') AS BIGINT) AS span_bytes
FROM read_otlp_traces('*/traces-*.pb')
ORDER BY span_bytes DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- The attributes that take the most bytes, from keys-level spans. Short
-- values are kept as they are, so they're left out here.
SELECT a.key, sum(CAST(json_extract(a.value, '$.bytes') AS BIGINT)) AS bytes
FROM read_otlp_traces('*/traces-*.pb'), json_each(span_attributes) AS a
WHERE json_extract_string(span_attributes, '$."tap.detail"') = 'keys'
  AND json_type(a.value) = 'OBJECT'
  AND a.key NOT LIKE 'tap.%'
GROUP BY a.key
ORDER BY bytes DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

duckdb-otlp reads raw OTLP protobuf and JSON. It's a young project, so pin its
version.

## Limitations

- The disk limit only counts what this collector writes, and what's already in
  the directory when a session starts. Another process writing to the same
  directory isn't counted.
- The directory can go over `max_disk_mib` by about one batch per writer,
  because a batch's compressed size is only known after it's written, and
  the four writers write at the same time.
- A file is rotated after the batch that takes it over `max_file_mib`. A
  single batch bigger than duckdb-otlp's 100 MB limit makes a file it can't
  read.
- When a pod or host goes away for good, the files it hadn't sent yet go with
  it. With files closing every 10 seconds, that's usually the last few
  seconds.
- Value sizes at the `keys` level, and `tap.body_bytes`, are approximations for
  comparing values, not encoded sizes.
- Only the `full` level is real telemetry. At `sizes` and `keys`, metrics lose
  the attribute values that tell their series apart.

## Migrating from the WebSocket processor

Earlier versions of this processor streamed rate-limited OTLP JSON to
WebSocket clients. That server, and its `endpoint` and `limit` options, are
gone. Clients now pull files over gRPC, from the endpoint set in `grpc`, and
`directory` is required.
